# Mobile, briefly {#sec-mobile}

The same Qt Quick application can run on Android and iOS. This chapter does not teach mobile
development; it shows what changes, so you can plan for it.

## Same code, different device {#sec-mobile-device}

What stays: your C++ layers, your QML, your build. What changes is the device around them:

- **Input.** Fingers instead of a mouse: no hover, larger touch targets, gestures.
- **Screens.** Small, dense, and rotating between portrait and landscape.
- **Lifecycle.** The system suspends your app when the user switches away, and may end it
  without warning. Save early, not on quit.
- **Files.** Each app lives in a sandbox; use `QStandardPaths` (@sec-paths), never fixed
  paths.

This is where the split from @sec-split pays off once more: logic stays in C++, and mostly
the views adapt.

::: {.more}
**Read more:** [Mobile development with Qt](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/mobiledevelopment.html)
:::

## Building for a device {#sec-mobile-build}

Mobile builds are cross-compiled with the platform's own tools: the Android SDK and NDK, or
Xcode for iOS. Qt provides a build for each platform, and the Qt Online Installer installs
them next to your desktop Qt. vcpkg builds your other dependencies for mobile triplets from
the same `vcpkg.json` (@sec-vcpkg).

::: {.more}
**Read more:** [Getting started with Qt for Android](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/android-getting-started.html),
[Qt for iOS](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/ios.html)
:::

## Permissions {#sec-permissions}

Using the camera, location, microphone or Bluetooth needs the user's consent, which the app asks for at run time.
Qt offers one permission API for all platforms:

```qml
import QtCore

CameraPermission {
    id: camera
}

Button {
    text: qsTr("Scan a sketch")
    visible: camera.status !== Qt.PermissionStatus.Denied
    onClicked: camera.status === Qt.PermissionStatus.Granted
               ? scanner.start() : camera.request()
}
```

Each permission must also be declared: in the app's `AndroidManifest.xml` on Android, and in
`Info.plist` on iOS, with a usage description that tells the user why. Ask for as little as
you need, at the moment you need it, so the user understands why.

::: {.more}
**Read more:** [Application permissions](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/permissions.html)
:::
